vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits across from me with his shoulders drawn inward, a posture I've come to recognize as his default. At fifty-four, he carries himself like someone much older-there's a heaviness to him that seems unrelated to his lean frame. He works as a senior administrator for the local council, a position he's held for nearly twenty years. By all outward measures, his life appears stable and orderly. But the tremor in his hands when he discusses his relationship tells a different story.

It started three years ago, though Marcus struggles to pinpoint exactly when things shifted. His partner, David, was charming initially-attentive in ways that made Marcus feel seen after years of emotional distance from previous relationships. But gradually, David's behavior became unpredictable. Criticism about small things escalated. When Marcus came home late from work, David would interrogate him. When Marcus disagreed about something trivial, David's voice would rise in a way that made Marcus's chest tighten.

The first time David hit him, Marcus remembers being almost shocked by how quickly it happened. They were arguing about finances-David wanted money Marcus wasn't comfortable spending. When Marcus said no, David shoved him against the kitchen counter. The impact knocked the wind from him. David apologized immediately, held him, said it would never happen again. Marcus believed him because he needed to believe him.

But it did happen again. Multiple times over the following months. Sometimes David would grab his arm so hard it left bruises Marcus would carefully cover with long sleeves at work. Other times it was open-handed strikes that left his face stinging. The worst incident came eighteen months ago when David threw him down the stairs during an argument. Marcus landed hard on his left shoulder and cracked two ribs. He told his colleagues at the council that he'd fallen-a story that felt easier than the truth.

Since leaving David eight months ago, Marcus has been rebuilding his life, but something fundamental has shifted inside him. He finds himself hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. When his new partner, Sarah, moves too quickly or raises her voice even slightly, Marcus's body floods with adrenaline. His heart races. He feels trapped. Just last week, Sarah reached toward him suddenly to adjust his collar, and he flinched so violently he knocked over his coffee. The shame afterward was almost worse than the fear itself.

At work, Marcus struggles to concentrate. He's always been meticulous-his desk organized, his reports thorough-but now he finds himself staring at spreadsheets for hours without absorbing information. His mind drifts to worst-case scenarios. He replays conversations obsessively, wondering if he said something wrong, if he provoked David somehow. Intellectually, he knows this isn't rational. He's intelligent enough to understand that he didn't cause the abuse. But knowing something intellectually and believing it in your bones are two different things.

Sleep is nearly impossible. Marcus lies awake most nights, his body tense, listening for sounds that might indicate danger. When he does sleep, he has nightmares-vivid replays of the violence, or sometimes newer scenarios where David finds him and the abuse resumes. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding so hard he thinks it might burst through his ribs.

What troubles Marcus most is how the trauma has changed his sense of self. He was always someone who prided himself on competence and control. Now he feels fragile, uncertain, like he's living behind a thin pane of glass that might shatter at any moment. The man who survived the abuse is still here, but he feels like a stranger to himself.
